<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-nass-autoplot</p>
</div>

The dashed line is the model-averaged prediction over the retained equations,
and the grey band is its 95% credible interval. The band is narrow at each dose
up to 1.25 and opens across the interval from there
to 2.5, where no dose was tested, and it remains
wide at 2.5, because the curve has to fall
somewhere in that interval and the data do not indicate where. The solid line is
the model-averaged *N(S)EC*, and the dotted lines are its bounds, at
0.42 and 1.91. The
axis is the one used for the raw-data figure, so the control keeps its marked
position, and the nine doses at or below 1.25 are
legible instead of stacked.

# A non-constant coefficient of variation {#a-non-constant-coefficient-of-variation}

In step 4 we compared the fitted spread with the observed spread within each
concentration. Here we work through a third response, whose coefficient of
variation changes systematically across concentrations although the family
fitted first assumes that it is constant. No convergence diagnostic detects this
departure.

In each family with a free dispersion parameter (e.g., `Gamma`, `Beta` or
`negbinomial`), that parameter is constant along the series unless the formula
specifies otherwise. For a `Gamma` family under the identity link, a constant
`shape` is a constant coefficient of variation (i.e., the standard deviation of
a replicate is a fixed multiple of the fitted mean at each concentration). Where
replicate variation does not behave in this way, a single `shape` is estimated
as a compromise between the low-concentration and high-concentration ends of the
series, and may describe neither.

## The assay

The `lum31` data contain the results of acute copper and zinc toxicity tests run
on the Lum-31 bioluminescent bacterial assay [@luter2025]. A suspension of
marine bacteria is dosed in a microplate well and its light output is read after
a fixed exposure, so the response is luminescence in relative light units.

Here we work through one plate of the copper series at 15 minutes (plate
`Cu 19Mar24 Rep1B`). A plate is a complete test (i.e., eleven concentrations by
four replicate wells). Because the plate reader sets its gain for each read,
plates are not on a common vertical scale, and taking a single plate avoids that
difference instead of modelling it. The group-level terms that handle the whole
assay, and the left-censoring that the blank correction requires, are described
in [*Grouping and factor
covariates*](https://open-aims.github.io/bayesnec/articles/example8.html).


``` r
data(lum31)
cu <- droplevels(subset(lum31, plate == "Cu 19Mar24 Rep1B" & minutes == 15))
c(wells = nrow(cu), concentrations = length(unique(cu$conc)),
  at_the_floor = sum(cu$censoring != "none"))
#>          wells concentrations   at_the_floor 
#>             44             11              1
```

This plate is one of two in the arm of
16 with
the fewest readings at the floor of the instrument (one of 44). A
reading held at a bound contributes a smaller spread than the well would have
shown, so a plate with many such readings would understate the quantity examined
in this section.

The four wells at a concentration share one cell of the plate, and readings from
one cell can vary together. Each fit below therefore includes `ogl(conc_group)`,
a deviation for each cell, so that the cell (and not the well) is the
observation at each concentration ([*Grouping and factor
covariates*](https://open-aims.github.io/bayesnec/articles/example8.html)
describes the term and how the model weights are computed under it). The
dispersion parameter then describes the spread of the wells within a cell.

A coefficient of variation computed from the four wells at one concentration
involves no curve, and cannot be inflated by any lack of fit in the mean. It
measures the same within-cell spread.


``` r
cv_obs <- tapply(cu$rlu_cens, cu$conc, function(z) sd(z) / mean(z))
round(cv_obs, 3)
#>     0.003 0.0137424  0.023888  0.044776  0.086552 0.1707008 0.3389984    0.6744    1.3458    2.6886 
#>     0.046     0.033     0.046     0.042     0.030     0.084     0.168     0.465     1.271     0.958 
#>    5.3742 
#>     0.876
```

The coefficient of variation is between 0.030
and 0.046 over the five lowest concentrations,
then rises without interruption to 1.271 at
1.3 mg/L, and
falls to 0.876 at the highest
concentration. The largest of these values is 28
times the control value, whereas a `Gamma` fitted with one `shape` returns a
single value for all of them.

## Fitting and screening the set

The copper response falls from its control, so `decline` is the candidate set
(the zinc series in this dataset rises above its control at low concentrations,
which is why `all` is fitted to it in *Grouping and factor covariates*).


``` r
gfam <- Gamma(link = "identity")
set.seed(17)
set_const <- bnec(rlu_cens | cens(censoring) ~ crf(log(conc), model = "decline") +
                    ogl(conc_group),
                  data = cu, family = gfam, seed = 17)
```


``` r
screened_const <- screen_models(set_const)
#> Dropping 2 of 11 candidate models that failed the sampler screen:
#>   -  ecxexp: 18 divergent transitions
#>   -  ecxwb1p3: 625 divergent transitions
#> Fitted models are: nec3param nec4param ecx4param ecxwb1 ecxwb2 ecxwb2p3 ecxll4 ecxll3 ecxflat
#> The fitted ecxflat curve does not fall to the control's 0.01 quantile within the predictor range for 7920 of 8000 draws. The NSEC summary is censored at 1.68: those draws keep their rank in it and are given no value.
#> The leave-one-group-out score has Pareto k above 0.7 for 2 of 11 levels of conc_group in ecxll4 (weight 0.32); 3 of 11 levels of conc_group in ecxwb1 (weight 0.23); 3 of 11 levels of conc_group in nec4param (weight 0.17); 4 of 11 levels of conc_group in ecx4param (weight 0.16); 4 of 11 levels of conc_group in ecxwb2 (weight 0.11). The scores of those levels are approximate; loo_controls = list(refit = TRUE) replaces them by refitting the equation without each level.
best_const <- pull_best(screened_const)
#> Highest-weighted model is ecxll4, holding 0.322 of the weight of 9 candidate models.
#> Pulling out model(s): ecxll4
```



15 equations were requested. `bnec_record()` shows
that 3 were excluded before fitting,
`ecxll5` failed to fit on these 44 observations,
and the screen removed 2 more (steps 2
and 3 describe all three mechanisms). Because a cell here is a whole
concentration, leaving out one cell removes a point on the curve, and the Pareto
*k* of such a score is often above 0.7 (the model-set check below counts the
retained equations with at least one such cell). Where it is, the model weights
are approximate. `amend(loo_controls = list(refit = TRUE))` would replace those
scores by exact refits, as in step 3, which requires one refit of an equation
for each cell above the cutoff, and we do not run it here.


``` r
copper_axis <- list(
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log", breaks = c(0.003, 0.03, 0.3, 3),
                     labels = function(x) signif(x, 2)),
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) {
    format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
  }),
  labs(x = expression(paste("Copper (mg ", L^-1, ")")),
       y = "Relative light units")
)
autoplot(screened_const) + copper_axis
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-disp-autoplot-const-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-disp-autoplot-const" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-disp-autoplot-const</p>
</div>

The curve is the model-averaged prediction over the retained equations, shown
with its 95% credible band and with the model-averaged *N(S)EC* marked. The mean
is described well, with the response remaining above
91
per cent of its control value up to
0.045 mg/L, and falling to below one per
cent by 0.34. The credible band
describes uncertainty in the fitted mean, and its width near the control
motivates a closer check of the variation between wells there. Comparing the
band with the range of four wells is not a test of the Gamma variance
assumption, however, and we use `check_fit()` for that comparison.

## Checking variability by concentration

A constant Gamma `shape` implies a constant coefficient of variation. We use
`check_fit()` to compare the observed spread within each concentration with the
spread of replicate responses simulated from the highest-weighted equation,
`ecxll4`. The model-set check below extends this
comparison to each retained equation.


``` r
cf_const <- check_fit(best_const)
cf_const[, c("group", "n", "obs_sd", "sim_sd", "sd_ratio", "ppp_sd", "control")]
#>        group n    obs_sd     sim_sd sd_ratio ppp_sd control
#> 1      0.003 4 48659.995 537620.904    0.091  0.997    TRUE
#> 2  0.0137424 4 34254.508 524139.572    0.065  1.000   FALSE
#> 3   0.023888 4 45273.800 520883.160    0.087  0.998   FALSE
#> 4   0.044776 4 40495.610 510924.631    0.079  0.999   FALSE
#> 5   0.086552 4 23064.931 432336.791    0.053  1.000   FALSE
#> 6  0.1707008 4 14403.575  91266.743    0.158  0.994   FALSE
#> 7  0.3389984 4  1143.009   3401.405    0.336  0.937   FALSE
#> 8     0.6744 4   221.393    271.833    0.814  0.639   FALSE
#> 9     1.3458 4   251.933    173.770    1.450  0.243   FALSE
#> 10    2.6886 4   513.008    196.850    2.606  0.044   FALSE
#> 11    5.3742 4   297.087    182.787    1.625  0.183   FALSE
```

`sd_ratio` is the observed spread divided by the simulated spread, so a value of
1 indicates agreement. Here it is between
0.05 and
0.09 over the five lowest
concentrations, then rises to a maximum of
2.61 at
2.7
mg/L, and 7 of the
11 groups are flagged. The fit simulates about
11 times the spread observed at
the control, and about 3 times too little where
the ratio is largest. A single `shape` cannot do both, and a constant
coefficient of variation requires it to.

## The dispersion sub-model

`disp("power")` writes `log(shape)` as a linear function of `log(mu)`, so that
the dispersion parameter becomes a function of the fitted mean instead of a
constant. The variance functions available, the families to which each applies,
and what the estimated exponent implies for a given family are described in
[*Single model
usage*](https://open-aims.github.io/bayesnec/articles/example1.html).


``` r
set.seed(17)
set_power <- bnec(rlu_cens | cens(censoring) ~ crf(log(conc), model = "decline") +
                    ogl(conc_group) + disp("power"),
                  data = cu, family = gfam, seed = 17)
```


``` r
screened_power <- screen_models(set_power)
#> Dropping 1 of 11 candidate models that failed the sampler screen:
#>   -  ecxexp: 61 divergent transitions
#> Fitted models are: nec3param nec4param ecx4param ecxwb1 ecxwb2 ecxwb1p3 ecxwb2p3 ecxll4 ecxll3 ecxflat
#> The fitted ecxflat curve does not fall to the control's 0.01 quantile within the predictor range for 7920 of 8000 draws. The NSEC summary is censored at 1.68: those draws keep their rank in it and are given no value.
#> The leave-one-group-out score has Pareto k above 0.7 for 3 of 11 levels of conc_group in ecxll4 (weight 0.51); 3 of 11 levels of conc_group in ecx4param (weight 0.46); 3 of 11 levels of conc_group in nec4param (weight 0.015); 3 of 11 levels of conc_group in ecxwb2 (weight 0.01). The scores of those levels are approximate; loo_controls = list(refit = TRUE) replaces them by refitting the equation without each level.
best_power <- pull_best(screened_power)
#> Highest-weighted model is ecxll4, holding 0.514 of the weight of 10 candidate models.
#> Pulling out model(s): ecxll4
```



The screen is run again, and not assumed, because a dispersion sub-model changes
the posterior from which each equation is sampled. Under the sub-model it
removed 1 of the
11 fitted equations, against
2 of 11
under constant dispersion. The highest-weighted equation is
`ecxll4`, with 0.51 of the
weight, against 0.32 for
`ecxll4` under constant dispersion, and
4 equations have a weight above 0.01, against
5.


``` r
brms::fixef(pull_brmsfit(best_power))[c("c0_Intercept", "c1_Intercept"), ]
#>               Estimate  Est.Error      Q2.5     Q97.5
#> c0_Intercept 4.8669396 0.33865682 4.1884883 5.5153802
#> c1_Intercept 0.8162669 0.06889577 0.6855049 0.9556025
```

`c1` is the exponent, and a value of zero corresponds to the constant-dispersion
model. The default prior bounds `c1` to the range 0 to 2 for a `Gamma` response,
so an interval well inside that range reflects the data and not the bound. The
coefficients of variation computed above provide an estimate of this exponent
that involves no fit, because a power law makes `log(cv)` linear in `log(mu)`,
with slope `-c1/2`.


``` r
conc_mean <- tapply(cu$rlu_cens, cu$conc, mean)
obs_slope <- lm(log(cv_obs) ~ log(conc_mean))
# Multiplying by -2 reverses the order of the bounds, so the names confint()
# supplied would be attached to the wrong ends.
setNames(-2 * c(coef(obs_slope)[[2]], rev(confint(obs_slope)[2, ])),
         c("c1", "lower", "upper"))
#>        c1     lower     upper 
#> 0.7689298 0.6579071 0.8799526
c(r_squared = summary(obs_slope)$r.squared)
#> r_squared 
#> 0.9646321
```

The fitted and observed estimates agree. The fit gives
0.82
(0.69
to
0.96),
and the wells give 0.77
(0.66 to
0.88). This agreement indicates
that the sub-model describes the replicate variation the design measured, and
does not absorb a failure of the curve elsewhere in the series. A
within-concentration standard deviation involves no curve, which is what makes
that comparison informative. Whether a power law is the right form for the
relationship is a separate question, which the regression addresses here with an
R-squared of 0.965 on
9 degrees of freedom.

## Checking the dispersion sub-model

We repeat the within-concentration check after fitting `disp("power")`.


``` r
cf_power <- check_fit(best_power)
c(flagged = sum(cf_power$ppp_sd > 0.95 | cf_power$ppp_sd < 0.05),
  groups = nrow(cf_power),
  control_sd_ratio = round(cf_power$sd_ratio[cf_power$control], 3))
#>          flagged           groups control_sd_ratio 
#>            0.000           11.000            1.251
```

For the highest-weighted equation, the number of groups flagged for scale falls
from 7 to
0, and the control ratio
changes from 0.09 to
1.25. Because the final
estimates use model averages, we also check each retained equation:


``` r
cf_const_set <- check_fit(screened_const)
cf_power_set <- check_fit(screened_power)
fit_scale_summary <- function(x, label) {
  parts <- split(as.data.frame(x), x$model)
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(parts, function(d) {
    data.frame(model = d$model[1], wi = d$wi[1],
               ctrl_ratio = d$sd_ratio[d$control],
               n_flag = sum(d$ppp_sd < 0.05 | d$ppp_sd > 0.95, na.rm = TRUE))
  }))
  names(out)[-1] <- paste(names(out)[-1], label, sep = "_")
  out
}
scale_summary <- merge(fit_scale_summary(cf_const_set, "const"),
                       fit_scale_summary(cf_power_set, "power"), all = TRUE)
round_cols(scale_summary)
#>        model wi_const ctrl_ratio_const n_flag_const wi_power ctrl_ratio_power n_flag_power
#> 1  ecx4param    0.162            0.094            7    0.459            1.226            0
#> 2    ecxflat    0.000            0.083            7    0.000            0.084            6
#> 3     ecxll3    0.000            0.083            7    0.000            1.260            0
#> 4     ecxll4    0.322            0.091            7    0.514            1.251            0
#> 5     ecxwb1    0.229            0.081            7    0.002            1.266            0
#> 6   ecxwb1p3       NA               NA           NA    0.000            1.261            1
#> 7     ecxwb2    0.112            0.093            6    0.010            1.211            0
#> 8   ecxwb2p3    0.000            0.082            7    0.000            1.197            0
#> 9  nec3param    0.000            0.082            7    0.000            1.180            0
#> 10 nec4param    0.174            0.091            7    0.015            1.223            0
high_k <- c(const = sum(attr(cf_const_set, "pareto")$n_high_k > 0),
            power = sum(attr(cf_power_set, "pareto")$n_high_k > 0))
```

The table gives, for each equation under each structure, its weight (`wi`), the
ratio of observed to simulated standard deviation at the control (`ctrl_ratio`),
and the number of concentrations flagged for scale (`n_flag`), with `NA` where
the screen removed the equation. Under constant dispersion the control ratio is
below 0.5 in 9 of the
9 retained equations, and under
the sub-model in 1 of
10. These counts show how far the
discrepancy found in the highest-weighted equation is shared by the rest of each
set. At least one cell has Pareto *k* above 0.7 in 8 of the
retained equations under constant dispersion, and in 10 under
the sub-model.

`plot()` draws each statistic against the spread that the fit simulates for it,
and takes both fits at once where a `model` column distinguishes the panels.
Because the response falls from about
1,060,000
relative light units at the control to about
198
at its lowest, we put the display on a logarithmic scale, as on a linear scale
the lower half of the series would be a row of points on the axis.


``` r
both <- rbind(cbind(cf_const, model = "constant"),
              cbind(cf_power, model = "disp(\"power\")"))
class(both) <- class(cf_const)
plot(both) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = function(x) {
    format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
  })
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-disp-checkfit-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-disp-checkfit" width="92%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-disp-checkfit</p>
</div>

Each bar is the 95% span of the statistic simulated from the fit, and each point
is the observed value. The observed means fall inside their bars under both
structures, although the bars are far wider under constant dispersion. This
agreement says little about the curve, because `check_fit()` simulates each
concentration with its fitted cell deviation, which can absorb a departure of
the mean from the curve. The spread of the four wells within a cell is
unaffected by that deviation, so the scale panels remain a test of the
dispersion structure, and they differ between the two structures. Under constant
dispersion the observed standard deviation falls below its bar at the
6 concentrations where the response is highest,
and the gap at the control is more than an order of magnitude
(48,700
observed, against a simulated span reaching
1,470,000).
Under the sub-model the bars close on the points, and the observed standard
deviations fall inside their bars, including that of the control
(48,700
against a span of
12,400
to
85,500).
A model can therefore reproduce the mean of each group and still be wrong about
the spread of all of them, which is the case described in the Overview, and here
the sub-model corrects it.

## The reported estimates

The estimates come from the screened set under the sub-model, shown here with
its credible band.


``` r
autoplot(screened_power) + copper_axis
```

<div class="figure" style="text-align: center">
<img src="vignette-fig-exmp9-autoplot-1.png" alt="plot of chunk exmp9-autoplot" width="80%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk exmp9-autoplot</p>
</div>

The curve is the model-averaged prediction over the retained equations, and the
band is its 95% credible interval, both returned on the recorded concentration
scale although the formula fitted `log(conc)`. The response remains above
91 per cent of its
control value up to 0.045 mg/L, is
at 16 per cent of it
by 0.17, and is below one per cent
by 0.34, so the whole decline
occurs over a factor of about
8 in
concentration. The vertical lines mark the model-averaged *N(S)EC* and its
bounds.

Compared with the constant-dispersion curve shown earlier, the band has narrowed
onto the observations, and the *N(S)EC* marked on the figure is lower. The
curves under constant dispersion and under the sub-model describe a common mean,
and differ in how wide each makes the posterior at the control, which is
measured below. The checks above were made on the highest-weighted equation and
on each retained equation, whereas the estimates are read from the screened
sets, because no single equation represents the model average.


``` r
copper_estimates <- rbind(
  constant_NSEC = nsec(screened_const),
  power_NSEC = nsec(screened_power),
  constant_EC10 = ecx(screened_const, ecx_val = 10),
  power_EC10 = ecx(screened_power, ecx_val = 10)
)[, c("Q50", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]
round(copper_estimates, 3)
#>                 Q50  Q2.5 Q97.5
#> constant_NSEC 0.110 0.049 0.150
#> power_NSEC    0.076 0.058 0.098
#> constant_EC10 0.085 0.016 0.139
#> power_EC10    0.076 0.068 0.094
```

The *NSEC* falls from
0.110 to
0.076 mg/L, a factor of
1.4.
The change arises through the quantity from which `nsec()` reads its reference,
which is the posterior of the control mean with any group-level deviation
excluded.


``` r
control_reference <- function(fit) {
  nd <- data.frame(conc = min(cu$conc), censoring = "none")
  post <- posterior_epred(pull_brmsfit(fit), newdata = nd, re_formula = NA)[, 1]
  c(sd = sd(post), cv = sd(post) / mean(post),
    reference_share = unname(quantile(post, 0.01) / mean(post)))
}
control_posterior <- rbind(constant = control_reference(best_const),
                           power = control_reference(best_power))
round(control_posterior, 4)
#>                 sd     cv reference_share
#> constant 172826.67 0.1709          0.6680
#> power     38535.97 0.0386          0.8954
```

For the highest-weighted equations, this posterior is
4
times wider under constant dispersion. Because `nsec()` sets its reference at a
lower quantile of it, the reference is at
0.67 of the
control mean under constant dispersion, against
0.90 under the
sub-model. A reference placed that far below the control is crossed further
along the curve, so the constant-dispersion fit returns the *less* protective
figure, and nothing in its sampler diagnostics indicates this.

The EC10 changes by less, from
0.085 to
0.076 mg/L, whereas its
interval narrows from a width of
0.123
to 0.026
mg/L. Because the EC10 is measured at a fixed fraction of the control mean, and
not at a quantile of its posterior, the variance assumption affects it through
the precision of the curve, and not through the placement of its reference. This
is the difference between the *NSEC* and the ECx described in the Overview.

A methods section should state the dispersion structure under which each
estimate was fitted, because constant dispersion and the sub-model return
different estimates from the same data.

# Summary

The sampler screen gave a different outcome for each fit in this vignette. On
the 2050 colour data at the default sampling length it removed
6 of the 12 fitted
equations under the uninformative priors and 7 of
12 under the regularising priors. On `nassarius` it
removed 8 of 11, and on the
copper plate 2 of
11 under constant dispersion and
1 of 11
under the dispersion sub-model. Which equations fail cannot be predicted before
the screen is run, so the equations removed, and the reasons, should be reported
for each fit; a prior choice that reduces failures in one equation may increase
them in another.

The diagnostic table separates inadequate effective sample size from divergent
transitions and failed initialisation. A longer run may resolve an ESS-only
failure, whereas divergences call for examining posterior geometry, priors and
parameterisation. Sparse concentration designs may contribute to these
difficulties, particularly for equations that estimate a lower asymptote or have
more curve parameters, but the diagnostics alone do not establish that
explanation. Excluding an equation at the stated cutoff is an analysis decision
that should be reported.

The variance assumption is the one that no sampler diagnostic detects. On the
`lum31` copper plate the observed coefficient of variation ran from
0.046 at the control to
0.876 at the highest concentration, and
the constant-dispersion fit passed the sampler screen for most of its equations
while its highest-weighted equation simulated about
11 times the spread observed at
the control. Adding `disp("power")` removed the groupwise flags for that
equation and reduced the model-averaged *NSEC* from
0.110 to
0.076 mg/L. A fit can
therefore pass the checks the sampler screen applies and still simulate the
wrong spread at the concentration from which both estimators are referenced.

Several decisions made around the fits also determine the estimates. For the
colour index, the family was chosen on the support of the data and not on a
test, the influence of the priors was assessed in step 5,
`asymptote_observed = TRUE` was declared although this design cannot verify it,
and the control was substituted before logging. For the counts, `binomial` was
retained after examining dispersion across the fitted equations. None of these
is a result the workflow produces automatically, and each is a decision that the
analysis needs to record.
